name: Anicka Yi
bio: Anicka Yi (born 1971) was born in Seoul, grew up in California and lives in New York. She came to art without formal training, and since the 2010s has built a practice around the senses that art usually ignores, especially smell, and around materials that are alive, perishable or unstable: bacteria, kelp, tempura-fried flowers, soap, ants, sweat and scent. She works with scientists and engineers; for You Can Call Me F (The Kitchen, 2015) she grew bacteria sampled from a hundred women. Her Hugo Boss Prize exhibition Life Is Cheap (Guggenheim, 2017) included a wall of bacteria and the scent of Asian American women and ants. For In Love With the World (2021), the Hyundai Commission at Tate Modern, she filled the Turbine Hall with floating machines, 'aerobes', that drifted like jellyfish and seeds through changing scents. Recent sculptures are lantern-like forms of dried kelp lit from within, some housing animatronic insects, and fibre-optic works that move like living things.
studyNotes: Work with what is alive or decaying. Bacteria grow, kelp dries, fried flowers darken; the piece keeps changing after it is installed.
Smell is a medium. She commissions scents as carefully as forms; ask what a room would smell like and why.
Machines as organisms. The aerobes and the motorised fibre-optic sculptures behave like creatures; she imagines how machines might live alongside us.
Collaborate with the lab. Much of the work depends on scientists, perfumers and engineers; the collaboration itself is part of the method.
